1. The animation shows a grid of squares, each one a historical case. Light squares are cases where a buyer was ahead after ten years. Dark squares are cases where a renter was ahead. The source line names FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The animation is labeled "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast". It is comparing buying with renting over a ten-year horizon.

2. The grid barely moves. Only the captions change. Frames 2–4 add "rent tag 6%: buyer ahead in 92.2%". Frames 5–6 replace that with "the share moves with the rent you assume". The dark column in the middle shifts slightly between frames, which may be a small change in the renter-ahead cases. I can't tell for certain from stills.

3. Under the 6% rent assumption, buying beat renting after ten years in about 92% of the historical cases. Renting won in about 8%. That share depends on the rent assumption, so a different rent figure would give a different percentage. The caption says it is history and not a forecast.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer could take away that the result is sensitive to the rent assumption, so they should test it against their own local rent and costs. They should also not treat 92.2% as a prediction.

5. The takeaway in 4 comes from the on-screen text, specifically "the share moves with the rent you assume" and "history, not a forecast". It is not my own conclusion. The animation does not tell the viewer to buy or to rent. Everything beyond those captions is my own reading.
